lead: A gas heated in a sealed rigid vessel stores energy; the same gas heated under a moving piston stores energy and also pushes the piston. The stored part is internal energy U. Adding the push work PV gives enthalpy H = U + PV. Both are state functions, fixed once the state is fixed. Their slopes against temperature, at constant volume and at constant pressure, are the heat capacities Cv and Cp. These two numbers give the heat in most closed-system heating steps and the work in most flow devices.
prereq: You need: the first law for closed systems (1.5), flow work in the steady-flow balance (1.6), and the state-function idea (1.2).

sections.h3: Internal energy U and enthalpy H

blocks.text: Internal energy U is the energy stored inside the boundary: the kinetic and potential energy of the molecules themselves, with the system at rest as a whole. U is a state function (1.2) and it is extensive (1.1), so doubling the gas doubles U. In this chapter small letters u, h and v are molar values, per mole, in J/mol and m³/mol; the same letters per kilogram (specific values, J/kg) appear in the flow chapters, and the unit tells you which is meant.

Enthalpy is defined as H = U + PV, where P is pressure in Pa and V is volume in m³. Since 1 Pa = 1 N/m², the product PV carries units of N·m, that is J, and adds cleanly to U. The molar form is h = H/n = u + Pv, with v the molar volume in m³/mol. Because U, P and V are all state variables, H is also a state function, and it is extensive like U.

Why add PV? In an open system the entering fluid must be pushed in and the leaving fluid pushes out; that push work is PV per mole (1.6). Grouping it with U gives one property, h, that appears naturally in nozzles, throttling valves, compressors and heat exchangers. Steam tables list h rather than u for exactly this reason.

Heat capacity is the heat needed to raise a unit amount by one kelvin. Which heat it is depends on what is held fixed. At constant volume the slope of u against T is Cv = (∂u/∂T)_v, in J/(mol·K). The subscript v means volume is held constant while T changes. At constant pressure the slope of h against T is Cp = (∂h/∂T)_p. The specific forms use small letters, cv and cp, in J/(kg·K).

Two slopes exist because the paths differ. Heat a gas in a rigid sealed vessel: no expansion work happens, so all the heat lands in internal energy and Q = ΔU. This rule, Qv = ΔU, holds for a closed system with only P-V work. Heat the same gas under a freely moving piston and the gas also pushes the piston, doing PΔV work.
Q<sub>p</sub> = ΔU + PΔV = Δ(U + PV) = ΔH
blocks.where: Q<sub>p</sub> is the heat added at constant pressure, in J; ΔU is the internal energy change, in J; P is the constant pressure, in Pa; ΔV is the volume change, in m³; ΔH is the enthalpy change, in J.

blocks.text: So for the same kind of process, Qp = ΔH. Read the two rules together: Qv = ΔU measures the change at constant volume, Qp = ΔH measures it at constant pressure. Some syllabi call Cv and Cp specific heats; the name is loose but common.

sections.h3: Ideal gas: u and h depend only on T

blocks.text: Joule's experiment (1.5) found no measurable temperature change when air at low pressure expanded into vacuum with no work and no heat. A real gas does change a little; for an ideal gas the change is exactly zero, so u depends on T alone, not on P or V. Then h = u + Pv = u + RT is also a function of T alone, where R = 8.314 J/(mol·K) is the gas constant.
Differentiate h = u + RT with respect to T at constant pressure: the R term contributes R, so Cp = Cv + R.
Cp − Cv = R  and  γ = Cp/Cv
blocks.where: Cp is the molar heat capacity at constant pressure, in J/(mol·K); Cv is the molar heat capacity at constant volume, in J/(mol·K); R = 8.314 J/(mol·K); γ (gamma) is the heat capacity ratio, dimensionless.

examples.question: 2.0 mol of an ideal gas with Cv = 20.8 J/(mol·K) is heated in a rigid closed vessel from 300 K to 400 K. Find ΔU, Q and W. The same gas is then heated from 300 K to 400 K under a constant pressure piston. Find ΔH, Q and W. Take R = 8.314 J/(mol·K).
steps: Constant volume, internal energy: ΔU = n Cv ΔT = 2.0 mol × 20.8 J/(mol·K) × 100 K = 4160 J.
Rigid vessel means no volume change, so W = 0 J. First law ΔU = Q − W gives Q = ΔU = 4160 J, added as heat.
Constant-pressure capacity: Cp = Cv + R = 20.8 + 8.314 = 29.114 J/(mol·K).
Enthalpy change: ΔH = n Cp ΔT = 2.0 mol × 29.114 J/(mol·K) × 100 K = 5822.8 J.
Cross-check: ΔH = ΔU + nRΔT = 4160 J + 2.0 × 8.314 × 100 J = 4160 + 1662.8 = 5822.8 J. Same answer.
Constant pressure gives Q = ΔH = 5822.8 J. The gas does work W = PΔV = nRΔT = 1662.8 J, which is the difference between 5822.8 J and 4160 J.
examples.answer: At constant volume: ΔU = 4160 J, Q = 4160 J, W = 0 J. At constant pressure: ΔH = 5822.8 J, Q = 5822.8 J, W = 1662.8 J.

traps: Using Cp for a constant-volume step. In a rigid vessel only Cv applies; at constant pressure only Cp applies.
Forgetting the moles. Cv in J/(mol·K) must be multiplied by n; if the value is in J/(kg·K), multiply by mass instead. The unit tells you which.
Treating h as heat. h is a state property in J/mol; Q is path-dependent in J. They are numerically equal only for a closed system at constant P with only P-V work.
Writing Cp − Cv = R after converting to specific heats. In J/(kg·K) the difference is R/M, with M the molar mass in kg/mol.
Applying Q = ΔU to an open steady-flow device. There the balance carries Δh plus kinetic and potential changes (see open systems and steady flow).

quiz.q: Define Cv and Cp with their units.
quiz.a: Cv = (∂u/∂T)_v, the slope of molar internal energy with temperature at constant volume, in J/(mol·K). Cp = (∂h/∂T)_p, the slope of molar enthalpy with temperature at constant pressure, in J/(mol·K).

quiz.q: Write the definition of molar enthalpy for a pure fluid and state its units.
quiz.a: h = u + Pv, where u is molar internal energy in J/mol, P is pressure in Pa, v is molar volume in m³/mol. The product Pv is in J/mol, so h is in J/mol.

quiz.q: Why does a gas absorb more heat at constant pressure than at constant volume for the same temperature rise?
quiz.a: At constant pressure the gas expands and does PΔV work on the surroundings, so part of the heat leaves as work. At constant volume no expansion work occurs and all the heat raises internal energy. Hence Cp is larger than Cv, by R for an ideal gas.

quiz.q: 1.5 mol of an ideal gas with Cv = 20.8 J/(mol·K) is heated at constant pressure from 300 K to 350 K. Find Q. Take R = 8.314 J/(mol·K).
For an ideal gas, Cp = 29.1 J/(mol·K) and Cv = 20.8 J/(mol·K). Find γ.
quiz.a: γ = Cp/Cv = 29.1/20.8 = 1.40, dimensionless. This is typical of a diatomic gas.

quiz.q: For an ideal gas, Cp − Cv = R exactly. For liquid water near 25 °C the difference is under 1 J/(mol·K), although Cp ≈ 75.3 J/(mol·K). Explain both observations.
quiz.a: For an ideal gas h = u + RT, so differentiating at constant pressure gives Cp − Cv = R: the difference is the P dV work of expansion, R per mole per kelvin. A liquid barely expands on heating, so that work is tiny and Cp ≈ Cv (for water about 0.8 J/(mol·K) apart). The general relation Cp − Cv = T(∂P/∂T)<sub>v</sub>(∂v/∂T)<sub>p</sub> is derived with the Maxwell relations.

quiz.q: Does the internal energy of an ideal gas change when it is compressed at constant temperature? Justify using Joule's experiment.
quiz.a: No. Joule's free expansion showed no temperature change with no work and no heat, so u depends only on T for an ideal gas. At constant T, u stays fixed and h = u + RT also stays fixed.

beyond: Not for the exam. In plant design enthalpy is the property you track through every heat exchanger and steam line, so steam tables are read in h, not u. Commercial simulators store ideal-gas Cp as a polynomial in T, then add a residual correction for real-gas behaviour. Searches that go further: mean heat capacity, residual enthalpy, and the departure functions used to correct ideal-gas Cp.
